chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara’s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma’s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara’s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva’s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
Meditation on superior intention. Contemplate the analogy about a drowning person and the onlooker versus the parent. The onlooker is like the mind of compassion, wishing the drowning person to be free of suffering. The parent is like the mind of superior intention, because they jump in to protect and save the drowning person.

Just explore this difference and what it would be like to have this superior intention for the people in your life and in your world. Transform your mind into superior intention, thinking, I will take personal responsibility to protect all living beings now. Just like the parent helps the drowning child now.

Just hold this strong intention, single-pointedly, deep in our heart. Then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Okay, so in person there's Anne P, Mimi, Fran, Ryan, Jose, Anne K, Mary Ann, David, Byron, and myself. Online there's Adriana, Ben, Dale, and Suzanne. Does anyone want to be the reader of Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life? We're going to move it forward actually today. It would be great if we could go from 26 to 36. Page 10 in the newest book. Fran, thank you.

shantidevaReading.text:
(26)	How can we possibly measure
The benefits of this jewel of a mind –
The source of joy for all living beings
And the cure for all their sufferings?

(27)	If the mere intention to benefit others
Is more meritorious than making offerings to the Buddhas,
What can be said of actually striving
For the happiness of every single living being?

(28)	Although living beings wish to be free from suffering,
They run straight towards the causes of suffering;
And although they wish for happiness,
Out of ignorance they destroy it like a foe.

(29)	For those who are deprived of happiness
And afflicted with many sorrows,
Bodhichitta bestows upon them boundless joy,
Eradicates all their suffering,

(30)	And even dispels their confusion.
Where is there virtue equal to this?
Where is there even such a friend?
Where is there merit such as this?

(31)	If even someone who repays a kindness
Is worthy of some praise,
What can be said of the Bodhisattva who helps others
Regardless of whether or not they help him?

(32)	If someone regularly, or even just once,
Gives food in a disdainful manner,
Which satisfies a few beings for only half a day,
People honour him or her as virtuous;

(33)	So what can be said of one who eternally gives
To countless living beings
The everlasting, unsurpassed bliss of the Sugatas,
Fulfilling all their wishes?

(34)	Buddha said that whoever generates an evil mind
Towards a Bodhisattva, a supreme benefactor,
Will remain in hell for as many aeons
As the moments for which that evil mind was generated;

(35)	But, for whoever generates a pure mind of faith,
The effects of good fortune will increase even more than that.
Even when Bodhisattvas are faced with great adversity,
Negativity does not arise; rather, their virtues naturally increase.

(36)	I prostrate to those who have generated
The holy, precious mind of bodhichitta;
And I go for refuge to those sources of happiness
Who bestow bliss even upon those who harm them.

This concludes the first chapter of Guide to the Bodhisattva’s Way of Life, entitled ‘An Explanation of the Benefits of Bodhichitta’.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
Thank you very much. So last week we were looking at superior intention. We were also looking at karma, and remembering that every action we perform follows the four characteristics of karma. For example, the definite relationship between cause and effect. The effects of actions increase, and so on. And that every action we perform leads to the four types of effect — the experience similar to the cause, environmental effect, ripened effect, tendency similar to the cause.

So we're trying to get the sense of what we do has consequences. We're really trying to live in that world of cause and effect, and connect that everything we do has consequences. Including not becoming enlightened has consequences, and not benefiting people has consequences. These are all actions. So we were kind of pondering that, and trying to use that to move our heart, and to inspire some more superior intention, greater mindfulness, and so on.

Anyone have anything to report? Could be on any of those things. It could be just your own musings, or ramblings, or a haiku, or whatever you'd like. Fran, yeah, please.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
So last Monday, at the end of the GP class, Doug was teaching, and he and I were closing up. And there was an episode that really has just sort of geared up my need to generate bodhichitta and remember its benefits. There's a woman who I've met here before. She's come in. Her speech is virtually unintelligible. And you can get a word here and there sometimes.

She's come in a few times before, and without going into detail of the other times, we were able to make out a little bit of what she wanted. She was always asking for something, not necessarily money, but sometimes money. And we were able to — she can get very loud — and we sort of quieted her down, and she would leave. And it was almost like a sense of relief. Okay, all right. We helped her. She's gone. That's it. It's done.

On Monday, she sort of snuck in as we were — I put the garbage out, and as I was coming back in, she snuck in sort of with me. Extremely agitated, extremely, extremely agitated. And first of all, I thought she was asking for money. I gave her a couple of dollars, but that wasn't it. And I was able to make out words like blessings and hug. Doug went and put his hand on her shoulder. It wasn't a hug she was looking for. The words supernatural powers came through.

But we were able to, at some point, I was like, all right. I don't even know her name, because most of her speech is unintelligible. So I was like, we're all going to leave together. We have to go home now. And she walked out. We sort of ushered her out, and then closed the door behind her because we weren't really quite ready to go.

And she went into this full-blown episode outside of the door with a hand flailing and speaking very loudly, totally unintelligible. I guess it was some — you might call it a manic episode — but whatever it was. And so we were a little bit — we felt trapped. Not trapped in here, but we didn't want to go out and agitate her even more, because we both agreed that we felt like we had betrayed her by saying, we're all going to leave together, and then we didn't.

It took a few minutes, and she started to ease her way up toward Nevins Street, little by little, talking. And we didn't want to pass by her. So it took us about 15 minutes until she went to the corner and then finally crossed over until we could get around to get to my car.

We were both so struck by — this is what a hell being's mind is like. This woman has a hell being samsara in her mind going on here. Nobody understands her. She can't say what she's doing. She's just flailing.

And this feeling of, this is an emanation of what we — it's either an emanation of something, so we understand, and this is probably just a fraction of what a real hell being is going through, but it's a hell being that we can understand. Or if it's actually a hell being breaking through on some level.

But for me, this week, in my six sessions, I generate bodhichitta, and I think about the benefits of bodhichitta. Times past, I never thought another bit about her after she left. This entire week she just kept appearing to me — that this is like the small part. That we're not just looking to solve the problems, we say, of this life, of this world, but this is like all the realms. This woman just kept appearing to me as this example of why I need to generate bodhichitta.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah. Yeah, it makes sense. Agreed. There's so many people like that. And many people we don't see, in other realms, who we need to protect too. So that's why we need to become a Buddha. It's very useful to use these experiences to motivate us, specifically with superior intention and bodhichitta. Thank you. Ryan, yes?

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text:
So as some of you have read, I wrote a long post about my frustration that I have all this free time but my time gets lost with my lack of structure in my life and distractions. So Fran was very kind and she wrote something about — she wrote two things. First she wrote, perhaps I need to work towards a purpose. And the second thing, she was trying to gently suggest me to open the center on Tuesdays for Harjo. Which I totally dismissed in a polite way. I didn't bite on her suggestion. And told her, yeah, probably gonna — I would love to do it on Thursday sometimes.

And then when I saw her, I read again and I was actually talking towards her purpose. And I'm like, I have a purpose — precious human life. Right? But this morning I was meditating on the train, and I'm like, do I live like I have the purpose of the precious human life? If I lived like the precious human life, I wouldn't waste two years of my life. I wouldn't let distractions overtake me.

And what does it even mean to live with the precious human life with full awareness? What's this purpose like? And then I had this conversation yesterday with Kyle about being a servant to others. And I was also meditating on this morning and I was like, aha, that's what we're doing here in the TTP.

So all this week we were like — talk about what you're cheating, what you're cheating, what you're cheating. It was a big word for me and I didn't really connect it towards me. And now I'm like, okay, we are training our mind to become a servant to others. I get it now. This is what we are doing here.

So I was having, supposedly, a purpose — I'm supposed to work to get contentment, getting rid of restlessness. No, that's maybe not my purpose anymore. Let me sit with the restlessness. If restlessness arrives, who said I have to be content? So this morning, the Harjo — right away there was an option for restlessness. There was a chair sitting in the wrong way. And my restless mind tells me, fix it. Because the GP will be in an hour and a half. So fix it now. And I'm like, no, it's okay if it's crooked. I don't have to fix it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text: Maybe the purpose is to be a servant for others. Like open the class, open Tuesdays for Harjo and others. So very grateful for Fran for nudging me, even if I first resented you for that. Thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Fran. Very good. Thank you very much. Just reframing that bodhichitta mind to servant. Instead of bodhisattva or something like that, just maybe resonates a bit more. Yeah, that's lovely. Anyone else? Dale, yes, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text:
Hi. So I'm just wondering, if you have a feeling — wait a minute, I could help this person — whether it's talking through something that you've been through before or physically help them or whatever, and the response back is either blah, blah, blah, kind of deflecting the help, kind of not welcoming the help. And so I'm wondering if at that point, obviously, you don't push it. You tried, you offered.

But I guess, right, what's important there is the intention of wanting to help. Helping feels wonderful to me, absolutely. I can't think of one thing that feels better, actually. But I'm wondering if that's the good way to think about it — that you had a good intention, but the timing wasn't right or whatever. The person was not in a place to accept it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah. I think that's right, Dale. Because if we can help someone, we should, of course. But if they're not responsive, then we don't have to worry about that, basically. And we just move on to someone else or some other activity. As long as our intention is good, then we can feel really happy with our action. Thanks, Dale. Adriana, yep.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text:
Okay, so this week, working on superior intention, I'm in a process of making a lot of plans to move, and it's all these logistics. And I was thinking about how the only good plan — oh, I wrote a haiku. Let me just read it because you said haiku.

Samsara's good plan / is to leave samsara now / let's go together.

So the only good plan you make in samsara that never disappoints you is the plan to leave samsara. So that's what I've been trying to think about. Like, every time I do one of the six sessions, every time I do a meditation, it's like, oh, now's my time to scheme and plan to get out of samsara. Because otherwise, we're planning all — our plan, by default, is like, let's stay. Let's keep finding things. Let's be here forever.

So I'm trying to make a different plan because superior intention felt very — it was a little difficult for me to grasp onto, but I just have to shift. I have to change plans. That's all.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks, Adriana. It's a nice point that you're making, that we have to keep our eye on the prize, which is — we really don't want to use our Dharma practice just to improve our samsara. We need to be aiming for liberation, enlightenment. And it's a really nice way to keep our six-session guru yoga alive and vibrant — to reconnect with that intention over and over again. Because it may be a little bit hard to maintain it at work, solving little problems in the day, running errands. It's just easy to get back into, I'm just fixing samsara.

Because that's what the Dharma Center is designed to do — to liberate people's minds. That's what it's aiming to do. It's almost not helpful at all to do anything other than that. Because people just die and the negative karma ripens and they just go into the next rebirth. So if we help people liberate their mind, that's really helpful. But if we just help them with ordinary things or whatever, it doesn't have a lasting impact.

Yeah, so we want to keep our personal eye on the prize and then help other people do the same. Thank you very much. Suzanne, yes?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text:
Hi there. I haven't been doing very well this week, so superior intention really seemed like a reach. I guess I could relate to what Grady was saying last week, like how he can't even manage the family and the staff. And I can't even manage just myself.

So I don't know. I guess I'm going to need Vajrayogini's help to bring everybody to enlightenment. I mean, I couldn't even manage to get to the class. I can't even manage really to sit up. And the one thing that I had — you know, we talked about this — my nephew was interested in karma, and I wanted him to go to a class. So he did. He finally went to a class today. He didn't make it through the whole class. He left it. For some reason, they started playing Liberating Prayer, and he bolted.

So I don't really know what to do about that. But I guess there's nothing I could do. That's just his karma, and let it sit for now. But yeah, I'm feeling totally out of control, I suppose.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah. What do you do to get back in control?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Well, unfortunately, it's very related to how I feel physically. Like right now, all my muscles are in spasm. My head is pounding. And unfortunately, the only thing that works is when I feel a little bit better because my mind cannot handle this level of discomfort physically. So then the emotions follow, and yeah, it's just not a good thing.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, so you tried to kind of wait out the intense pain and discomfort. Is that right?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Pretty much. I mean, I don't think I did any of my six sessions today. But I did do something, and I did my mantras. I did something, and I'm here, kind of. Probably only because I don't want to lose my streak. So I don't know if that's a good reason.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: It's a very good reason. No, keep that up. Do you know what number you're at now?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Well, whenever we first started TTP. Four and a half years almost, right?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: September 2021. Yeah, it's over 200 straight TTPs. It will never ever be broken by anyone. So just keep it going. It will be truly unbreakable. It might not be broken by many people in any Dharma center.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I can start again and try to break it on my own.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Oh, that's true, that could be fun. No, keep making it go up. Yeah, thanks, Suzanne. I appreciate you sharing that. In those cases, is there something that could take no effort on your part that could be somewhat useful and virtuous? The advice that's been given to people who have been really ill, like in hospital, has been sometimes just to play one of the audiobooks — like the Modern Buddhism audiobook or something like that.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Yeah, I do. That's sort of the thing.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, and that's nice because you don't have to do anything.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I listened to the second part of last week's class this morning.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, okay, that's fantastic. So you have those kinds of strategies. Because sometimes our mind is just so sapped or the pain is so strong that it's very hard to do something that involves us. And so that's where having something like a little bit passively happening and washing over us can be really useful. So that's great — listening to an old class or prayers. Or even just having Buddha images around that can imprint our mind and just looking at them.

And it's good for us all to think about that. If we haven't been in those cases where our pain is at a certain level or we can't even think — what are we going to do? How can we have some virtue going on in those moments? Thanks, Suzanne. Mimi, and then David. And then we'll hop into the text.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text:
So I've been thinking about superior intention. And I hope Juliana doesn't mind me sharing this. So this week has been a week for thinking about Juliana. So many beautiful things have happened.

So I don't know if many of you know, but Juliana came to live with me when she was three. And she's going to now be 18. And when she first came — I'll keep it brief — but when she first came I really didn't think that she was going to stay. She came with her father. And her father and Julie's mother had had a disagreement. And I just thought it was a boyfriend-girlfriend thing and that Sebastian would be going back to Colorado with his little girl.

But it didn't end up that way, because the days and the months just kept going. And there was Julie. So I realized one day that Juliana was going to stay. And she used to — because we had a small apartment — Julie used to sleep with me. And Sebastian slept on the air mattress in the living room.

And I was like, maybe midnight or something, Julie was fast asleep, and I just suddenly realized that there was nobody in the family except me to take care of her. And I had to be the one to step up and take care of her. And I made a promise to her that night. Basically it was like a covenant, like a vow. And I just told Julie that I would be her protector. And that I would take care of her and protect her, even against sometimes her father. And that I would ensure that she would be safe.

And I've kept my vow. And now she got into college. And I'm just beside myself in happiness. But if I was able to step up and say, I will be your protector, then I can do that as a Buddhist. And I can do that for others.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thank you so much, Mimi. This is a lovely example and an analog that we can all try to aspire towards with respect to all living beings. Because that decision — it's a bit different than a determination. It's like a decision or a vow. Like, I am going to do this. Not I'm aspiring to do this, but I am going to do this. That's the mind we want to get to with respect to becoming a Buddha for the benefit of all.

And to be able to do that with one person is actually amazing and heroic. And many of us have not done that with respect to one person, even, to just make that decision. And then to do that for all living beings — that's the bodhisattva mind. Which is an incredibly — yeah, it is a heroic, wondrous, jewel of a mind.

It's like in the bodhisattva vow we make a promise to become enlightened for the benefit of all. And I always remember a teacher of mine saying in a festival, she kept saying, 'How's your promise going? You promised to become a Buddha for the benefit of all. So how's it going?' And it was very touching for me. I always remember that. Because it's like, oh yeah, I did promise. So am I treating it like a decision, like you did with your granddaughter? Am I treating my bodhisattva vow as a decision, as a real promise? Or am I treating it as an aspirational 'let's go for lunch sometime' kind of thing, which is not even really a wish — it's just something we say to be polite. What is it?

And how can we make it a promise, a decision like that? Because our mind has the capacity to do that. It's incredibly powerful. Thank you very much, Mimi. David, last one.

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, I enjoyed — a little feedback maybe. I enjoyed thinking that no one else is going to do it. It was something you mentioned last week, that we ourselves have to basically become enlightened to liberate all other beings. Because it was really helpful. Because I think normally I have this experience of like, I'll do kind of my part, but there's a lot of factors at play here.

And I feel like when your mind has ignorance functioning, then it seems like things are random, and that things just kind of happen. And we can influence things to some extent, but not really fully. And so it was really helpful actually to think that, no — there's no randomness at all. There's no chance, even in the slightest. My enlightenment will only happen if I cause it to happen. And same with liberation of everyone else. And it really helped focus.

And at times it could feel a little bit overwhelming, because I feel like it's such a tall order. But I also found thinking about one of the characteristics of karma — that the results of actions increase — to be really helpful for that. And like, who knows what a bundle of virtuous actions could lead to. And I think all of us could think about that — like first time we set foot into this center, for example. Think about that one little action and all the things that have cascaded from that for each of us. And so if we do enough small things in the right direction, then just to be humble about where that could lead. And we don't really want to put a cap on it.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah, thanks so much, David. Those are great points. So just kind of keeping that thought going — no one else is going to do it. Yeah, it's a great mantra. No one else is going to save the living beings of samsara. It's my job.

And the more we think that, the better things become. And the more clear they become. And then it just helps us see like, oh, I just don't want to do it. Which is just great to see that. Oh, I just don't want to actually. Oh, okay, cool. Now I can work with something. I'm just fully honest. I just don't want to actually get on with it. I don't want to help them. Great. Then we can make some change. Because we're actually seeing the laziness or ignorance in our mind directly.

It's much more problematic if it's there and operating, and we're going, yeah, I want to. That's much more complicated because it's self-deception. Versus, oh, I just don't want to. Oh, okay, good. Now I know. All right, let me get moving on that.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
And then about the results of actions increase. This is definitely true. It's just so crucial. It's just about staying in the game. The results of actions increase. So all the good karma we make, it just keeps growing and increasing like crazy. But we do have to stay in the game. So we give it enough space to increase.

It's like some of these famous investors or whatever. When people ask them what their secrets are, they're like, yeah, we're not smart, really. We just stayed in the game. We put some money in some fund 50 years ago, and we just decided not to move it. And everyone else just kept moving it. And now we have $100 billion or whatever. And everyone else is broke. We just stayed in the game.

It's just an analogy, right? But it's helpful to think the same with our karma. We've just got to stay in the game. We've got to have a long-term view. And if we just stay with it, stay in our refuge, and let our karma keep growing, it will just eventually, exponentially explode.

So even though it feels like a big deal — I'm going to become a Buddha for the benefit of all, whoa, that's a big order — we don't want to extrapolate linearly. It's not a linear extrapolation. Our karma growing and increasing is an exponential curve. It whips up vertically. But we have to give it a little time to do that.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Okay, thank you very much. Let's take a look at the text. So we were looking at the six-session guru yoga, and then we were talking about being guided by love. These are some themes that we've been using. And then with respect to being guided by love, we've just sprinkled in some other sutra teachings — both thinking about renunciation, uncertainty, which can help us be guided by compassion, not just love. And then superior intention, and also looking at the understanding of karma, which is not just being guided by love, not just being guided by compassion, but being guided by a decision to protect everyone and take responsibility.

And so now we're moving into bodhichitta specifically, which is the most educated love and compassion.

So Geshe-la is here on page 44, developing bodhichitta. 'Through contemplation and examination we'll discover that only a completely perfect being who has awakened from the sleep of ignorance, a fully enlightened Buddha, has the complete power to liberate others from their suffering. The truth of this becomes clear when we think about the attributes a true liberator of others must have. Such a being would have to possess the four characteristics of an awakened one:

1. Freedom from all obstructions preventing liberation and omniscience
2. Great skill in liberating living beings from their suffering
3. Compassion for all living beings without discrimination
4. Benefiting all living beings whether or not they've helped him.'

These are things that we absolutely need to memorize. These are like a non-negotiable, have-to memorization items. There's no excuse. There is no reason we should not learn these off by heart. Because they are the four characteristics of a Buddha that, by thinking about, turn us from just being compassionate to a bodhisattva.

It's specifically these four characteristics of a Buddha that we think about, that make us think, ah, I need to become a Buddha for the benefit of all. So we absolutely need to know these. It's like our childhood telephone number or something like that. Hard-wired into our skull. 609-443-4606. Hard-wired. It's never going to go anywhere. If I lose my memory one day and become completely senile, I will be able to say it. Things like this need to be like that for us.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
So we can start thinking about them a little bit. Freedom from all obstructions preventing liberation and omniscience — when we see that, we want to ask, why is that necessary? Great skill in liberating living beings from their suffering — why is that necessary? Compassion for all living beings without discrimination — why is that necessary? Benefiting all living beings whether or not they have helped us — why is that necessary?

They are somewhat straightforward. But we want to get the sense of, with each one, I really want this. I really, really want this skill, this attribute. Part of doing that is thinking about how annoying and frustrating and powerless it is to not have these attributes.

For example, benefiting all living beings whether or not they have helped us. You can think how annoying and frustrating it is — just so petty and miserable and ordinary — to just my side versus your side, or only wanting to help the people we like. A little bit like, you pat my back, I pat yours. That's a miserable place to live in. It's like doing favors for people because they do favors for us. We're like a mobster or something like that. Bodhisattva, mobster. 'Yes, I will benefit you who helped me. I'll do you a favor.' I don't want to live like that. I want to have a completely open-hearted mind.

Compassion for all living beings without discrimination is related — it's trying to find all the people that we have scorn for, that we don't like, that we don't care about, that we don't think about, and thinking how tiring that is, to live that way, and how contradictory it is for our bodhisattva mindset, and how limiting it is to neglect so many living beings.

Great skill in liberating living beings from their suffering — it's just seeing how powerless we are right now. We've talked about this a bit, but it is very useful to meditate on our profound inability to help people, and the examples where we've tried to help and it's made things worse.

Freedom from all obstructions preventing liberation and omniscience — if we don't know what enlightenment is for ourself through removing all of our obstructions, then how can we lead other people to the same place? We don't even know where we're leading them to. And this helps us know all paths and all routes to enlightenment, and know people's karma specifically, and their tendencies and their mental states.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
So we're trying to take these and really get a feeling — I want each one of them. I want impartiality, I want to be able to help people regardless if they've helped me. I want great skill. I want freedom from the obstructions to liberation and omniscience. I want all of those. Not because Buddha said so, but because I personally want them. And part of the reason I want them is because I understand the pain and limitation and the powerlessness of not having them.

Okay, so let's all ponder these four, and then ponder some ways to move these forward a little bit. What's step one, moving each one of these forward? What's going to get us from where we are today to incrementally further on any of these four?

For example, great skill. How do you get great skill? You fail. You practice trying to help people and repeatedly failing over and over again. And you learn. Then you've got to overdo it, and you underdo it, and you get a little too wrathful sometimes, and you get too gentle sometimes, and you start to learn, and you practice becoming more skillful. We can't get more skillful on the sidelines, that's for sure. You've got to practice and fail.

Part of great skill is understanding the differences between people, and the diversity of people, and what they need, and what they're like. So it might be like our first step in increasing our skill is really becoming aware of the different needs and proclivities of different types of people we meet, and not treating all people like a two-dimensional object.

Most of us, what we do is we just project what we are and what we like on everyone else, and then give them what we like. Which is completely wrong. Because we're all weird. You're not on TTP because you're just completely normal. So if we're going around slapping that on everyone we meet, we're going to be missing the boat a huge amount of time.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
And so, it's like a psychological development. It's like having a theory of mind. It's supposed to happen when you're like five or seven. You're supposed to know other people have minds that are different than yours. So as a Buddhist, and trying to help people, we need to be able to do that. People are different than us. So they need different things, and they respond differently. So what do they need? And what are their proclivities? What are their strengths? What are their weaknesses? How can we help them?

We can contemplate, for example, Dorje Shugden's four compatriots, who represent pacifying, increasing, controlling, and wrathful actions. And the permutations of all those four actions. We can think, do I know the situations where I pacify? Do I know the situations where I increase? Do I know the situations where I support controlling actions, like helping people control their delusions? Do I know the situations where I need to be wrathful? And do I know how to get there and do that?

Do I have skill in performing those four types of actions? Am I even discriminating like that? Or are we just winging it when we talk to people, interact with people, or try to help people?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
One of the easiest ways, actually, to increase our skill is to increase our quick wisdom through relying on Buddha Manjushri, where we mentally recite DHI over and over again. I'll read out the transmission from it in the next session just so I don't wing it. But basically, on a breath, you recite DHI DHI DHI DHI DHI DHI over and over again, and you imagine you get all these blessings from Buddha Manjushri in the form of orange light. And it pours into this little DHI, and then you swallow it, and it's like a blessed syllable, Manjushri's seed syllable, and it mixes with your heart and your mind, and you get quick wisdom.

And this is an aspect of skill, because quick wisdom is what helps us make a decisive, right choice in a moment. So Manjushri's blessings can help us do this. And this will increase our skill a lot. Because usually, like with Fran's example earlier of this lady, whom I also had the privilege to interact with a couple of times, often we need to call on some skill in moments like that, that involve a pretty much instantaneous action and response.

The point I'm trying to make is that with these four, we admire them, we appreciate them, we want them, and then we want to be practical about asking, how can I move them forward? To get the qualities of Buddha, we don't just sit there with nothing. And then all of a sudden, we're a Buddha one day. Boop! We have a perfect experience of all these skills. No, we become a Buddha by working, growing these skills. It's a spectrum. We start creating the grooves in our mind to be a Buddha by working on these four skills today.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
And then we looked briefly at the eight precepts of aspiring bodhichitta. These are: 1) To remember the benefits of bodhichitta six times a day. 2) To generate bodhichitta six times a day. 3) Not to abandon any living being. 4) To accumulate merit and wisdom.

And then the four precepts that prevent the aspiring mind from degenerating in future lives: 5) Not to cheat or deceive our Preceptors or Spiritual Guide. 6) Not to criticize those who have entered the Mahayana. 7) Not to cause others to regret their virtuous actions. 8) Not to pretend to have good qualities or hide our faults without a special, pure intention.

This last one is just about not being pretentious, or having concealment. This doesn't mean we need to shout from the rooftops our inadequacies, which is often its own coping mechanism. This self-deprecating, insecure behavior — before anyone else notices, I'm going to shout it out to everyone so they know that I know. That's its own deluded thing. The point is just we're not projecting something that's not true, nor actively suppressing something that is true out of some deluded mind.

A fun activity, a little puzzle to solve, is like, why are these the eight vows? Why are these last four specifically chosen as the essential vows for preventing the aspiring mind from degenerating? We have to chew on that a little bit.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
The main conclusion is just that we want to be guided by bodhichitta. We want to grow our bodhichitta through thinking about the four qualities of a Buddha. That's the main thing. The rest is extra. Let's make sure we don't miss the point here.

A reminder that Sumit's half-day course on emptiness is next Saturday. So come along if you can. And then our Dorje Shugden empowerment is the 7th of March. Please do mark that on your calendar. Bring your round yellow hat. You get in half price if you bring your round yellow hat with you.

Let's dedicate now. We can think through the virtues we've collected, through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. You can make any personal prayers. Okay, thank you. We'll come back at 6:16 approximately.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Okay, welcome back. So let's just finish up with these eight vows and specifically let's look at cheating and deceiving the spiritual guide. And what we'll do is we'll just have a little debate.

The people on this side of the room — Byron, Jose, Mary Ann, David, plus Ben and Suzanne — your point that you're trying to make is: breaking a vow is cheating or deceiving your spiritual guide.

The other side — Anne P, Mimi, Fran, Ryan, plus Adriana and Dale — your argument is: breaking a vow is not cheating or deceiving your spiritual guide.

Let's get an example of a vow. We have a bodhisattva vow to help the sick, or to not disregard — I think doing nothing to help the sick is like breaking the vow. So a sangha friend is sick and they ask you to come visit them. And you say, no, I will not. So, this side plus our two online people are saying that's cheating and deceiving your spiritual guide. Other side is saying you can still say that's breaking a vow, but it's not cheating or deceiving the spiritual guide.

teaching.speaker: Byron
teaching.text: Hello, hello. Our spiritual guide's mind is interwoven inextricably with our own. If we know that we have broken a vow, we took the vow knowing what the vow meant. We have now broken that vow. We know that we've broken it. Our spiritual guide knows that we've broken it. That is definitely a betrayal.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: You have cheated your spiritual guide. Okay, there we go. Adriana, yeah, you look feisty out there.

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text: Our spiritual guide is a fully enlightened Buddha who relates to us as having Buddha nature, seeing our pure potential. When we break our vow and have to face the consequences and purify our own faults and negativities — it is technically impossible to conceal anything from our spiritual guide because they are fully omniscient.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, very nice. Thank you. Others? Mary Ann, yep.

teaching.speaker: Mary Ann
teaching.text: I don't know about concealing or deceiving, but you're definitely cheating them out of their mission and your mission — the whole project to liberate all living beings. That is being cheated out of good stuff.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yep, thank you. So you're kind of emphasizing the cheating part. Yes, Dale, thank you.

teaching.speaker: Dale
teaching.text: Okay, so just — this seems very simple to me, but you have a friend who's sick and you want to go see them, but what if you're sick with COVID? You're sick yourself. Do you say, no, no, no, I can't break my vow, I've got to go — and then what? Get that person sick? So I think if it's genuinely you're concerned about getting the other person sick when they're already sick, that's my thought.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: All right, so you're kind of more making the point of like you're not really even breaking the vow.

teaching.speaker: Dale
teaching.text: Well, you are breaking the vow, but isn't there any kind of reason that it would make sense?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, and part of all these vows are without good reason. So it would be like not helping that person who's sick with no good reason for doing so. Fran, and then David after that.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: So first let me say I'm not sure I really believe this because I want to be on the other side. But I think it has a lot to do with your intention, that if you're really saying — again, good reason or even just thoughtlessly not helping somebody who's sick and you're off running doing something else and it's not your intention to deceive your spiritual guide — then you're not.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, I think that's a big crux of the matter — about what's the intention. David, yes, thanks.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: I would just say that our spiritual guide doesn't give us — the vows are very carefully cultivated and our spiritual guide doesn't give us vows that we're not ready for. And if we take them, then we should be prepared to keep them. And it is kind of a promise and we shouldn't take that lightly. And breaking a promise — like if you promise your friend, I'm going to help you when you need me, and then you don't — that's a betrayal. And so maybe we should take it a bit more seriously maybe than we do.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. So you're kind of saying when you take the vows originally, it's a promise. So not keeping it is breaking a promise, which is the same as a betrayal. Anyone else we haven't heard from? Mimi?

teaching.speaker: Mimi
teaching.text: I don't think Geshe-la would be mad. I don't. We're just kind of like babies, right? Yes, it's important to take the vow, take it seriously. But sometimes I forget to do my Vajrayogini mantras and I've taken the promise to do it every day. And Geshe-la has always said, just try. So I think we have to have the intention to keep it. But I don't think we should beat ourselves up if we don't do it. Not in a mean way.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, that's a nice point, Mimi. Fran, please.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: When we take these vows, are we specifically taking them to our spiritual guide? Are we directing them at our spiritual guide? Or is it something that we're vowing to ourselves?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: No, your spiritual guide is giving you those vows. Very explicitly giving you your vows. Yeah. I don't know if I'm actually that satisfied with either side. Or either of the arguments that have been made. No offense. Where's Ben?

teaching.speaker: Ben
teaching.text: I mean, I think it's straightforward, right? If you promised something, and then that's not what you did, the promise was deceptive.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, okay, so you're kind of similar to what David was saying about the promise part. Adriana, yeah?

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text: The bodhisattva vow is not made of glass. It's made of clay.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Mmm, yeah. Do you want to say more about that?

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text:
Yes. So when we break a vow, it's not like glass shatters and we've done irreparable harm. It's like clay, and we try again. And as Mimi said, Geshe-la just asks us to try. He's never asking us to be perfect. He's asking us to try.

And we take the vows over and over again so that we create enough merit in our minds to fulfill them. But when you first take them, the preceptor will say, don't worry if you don't understand it. Just hang out and enjoy, and gradually you will come to understand them.

I really struggle with this word cheating. Because it's not like I'm saying, Geshe-la, can you lend me $5 and I'll pay you back tomorrow, and then I give him back a fake $5 bill. That's not what's happening. That's cheating. But if I just forget and say, Geshe-la, I'm sorry I forgot, I'll bring you tomorrow — eventually I remember. Or what if I run out of money and say, I'm so sorry, I have to pay you $1 every day next week. I think that's what we're doing. We're just trying our best.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, thanks, Adriana. So this is kind of getting to the point here. When we ponder these Dharma questions, it's very helpful to think about them more deeply. The question is — why is this vow here? That's what I was sort of wishing someone was going to mention. What's its practical purpose? Why is it a vow to not cheat or deceive our spiritual guide? It's not just a rule. It's a Dharma teaching to help us become enlightened.

When we start to probe that, we start to see this is a practice. It's a verb. It's like an invitation for a conversation with our spiritual guide, an ongoing trust and conversation and openness. And it's saying, always rely on your spiritual guide. Always have an open conversation. Always have a chat going on, like a little thread, like you do with your family or your best friends. Like a little ongoing group chat. Always keeping the thread open. Never closing it off.

Sometimes we do cut ourselves off externally from outer friends for different reasons. Sometimes we insulate ourselves, or we go in, or we hide, or hibernate. That can happen for days or months or years. It's kind of saying, never do that with your spiritual guide, though. They're always with you like a best friend, day in and day out, through thick and thin. They're like the only friend that goes with us into our next life. Every other friend disappears. But the spiritual guide goes with us to our next life, and then the next life.

So the intention of the vow is: never turn away, never forget our spiritual guide. Never hide from them. Keep a conversation going always, even in our worst day, in our lowest state. Have the chat going on. Like, hey, Buddhas, I'm a mess today. Or, hey, I'm going to break this vow right now, and I'm so sorry. I just got nothing else in me. But I'm just telling you. Because I'm keeping the flow going.

Sometimes we just get absolutely walloped by a delusion, but we can still keep the conduit open and say, I'm so sorry, I'm a mess. I got nothing. But I love you, my guru, and I know you love me, and you'll be with me on the other side of this. And then you hold their hand. And it's a mess, and it's not a great moment. But not necessarily cheating or deceiving.

This is what Adriana was getting at about the clay. When we get bodhisattva vows and tantric vows, the principal vow is the intention to keep it. That's level one. Level two is then keeping it flawlessly and perfectly. That's aspirational. The reason it's called clay is because the intention to keep it is the actual vow. So if we're not able to do level two, it's not actually breaking the vow if we didn't give up our intention.

If we abandon the intention completely, that is officially a little bit like turning on our spiritual guide. That's what Byron, David, and Ben were getting at about the promise. We need to be clear what exactly is the promise. The promise is the intention to keep the vows. It's not the rule itself.

Whenever we probe these Dharma questions, we always want to ask, how is what I'm looking at a practice? Not cheating or deceiving our spiritual guide — that's a practice. A practice of keeping an open conversation going, an honest connection going throughout the day. That's what we're being invited to do.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: Not keeping that conversation going, would that be considered holding wrong views? Denying the existence of the Buddhas?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Not necessarily. It could just be forgetting. Just forgetting. It doesn't need to be such a grave thing.

Holding a wrong view is overtly holding a view that's detrimental to our liberation. Like purposely holding it. More clearly, it's rejecting a Dharma truth. So if you just forget the conversation with your spiritual guide, you're not necessarily saying, there are no past and future lives, period. That's holding a wrong view. Karma is not true, period. That's holding a wrong view. Those are really detrimental and complicated actions.

Simply forgetting — yeah, we want to work on that. But we might just not have good mindfulness. In which case, we should give ourselves a break and work on improving our mindfulness. Ryan, yeah?

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: What if I've never chosen, never made a sit-down, officially as a meditator, or chosen who is my spiritual guide? I mean, I know the Kadampas here, I've chosen Geshe-la, but I've never really thought about it. I mean, the closest one, if I would have to choose right now, would be probably Buddha Shakyamuni, or Je Tsongkhapa, that I do the Heruka practice to him. I feel very close to them. Buddha's teachings, you know? So, yeah.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, it's a nice question. Both who is our spiritual guide, and if we don't feel like we've kind of created that root, how do we go about creating that root? Because it's the root of the whole spiritual path — reliance on a spiritual guide.

So technically, our spiritual guide is whoever we get our highest sutra or tantra empowerments from. This is like one technical definition — our root guru. It doesn't necessarily mean the physical human who's there. It might be the Buddha who's working through them. But this is one kind of definition.

The other is thinking it's someone who sets a perfect example and leads people on correct paths to enlightenment. So they set a perfect example, and they lead people on correct paths. So that's a qualified spiritual guide.

So you mentioned Buddha Shakyamuni and Je Tsongkhapa, right? Yep, those are — they set perfect examples, they lead people on paths to enlightenment and liberation. So they're great choices as a guru, as a spiritual guide. And they're actually the same person. So you can keep it a bit more simple.

But what's important to remember is, if we rely on them, then there must be emanations of them in our life who are helping us. And that's who we want to find. The practice of reliance on the spiritual guide is about finding — where's the human that I can talk to and rely on?

Basically, if Buddha Shakyamuni became enlightened to lead all living beings to that same state, he could not stop appearing in human form to connect to people and guide people. He couldn't stop himself, actually. He would have to continually appear in the form of countless emanations, guiding people to the same state. If he didn't do that, he's not a Buddha. That's not very kind, right? And he has the power — that's why you become a Buddha. You can emanate forever countless spiritual guides and emanations to lead people to the same state.

So we have to infer — if we want to rely on Buddha Shakyamuni or Je Tsongkhapa as our spiritual guide, that means they're Buddhas. If they're Buddhas, then they have to have human emanations appearing in our world. If they don't, they're not Buddhas. So then we shouldn't rely on them as a spiritual guide.

So then it's on us. I need to find where those emanations are so I can have a chat with them and be guided by them and helped by them. Because it's hard to be exactly, precisely guided just by Buddha's truth body or enjoyment body. We can't see that. We can't see it with our eyes. We can't have a full-blown conversation.

If we can, that means we've basically attained tranquil abiding, which is fantastic. And if anyone has, then yeah, you can avoid the human spiritual guides and just do that — have chats with Buddhas. If we've not attained tranquil abiding, we cannot just have a chat directly with Buddha's enjoyment body. We might say something is speaking to me, but that could just be a spirit. We don't know. We have no idea what's speaking to us through the ether. How do we know? It could be anything.

So we need to find a living representation of our spiritual guide, of the Buddhas, who can guide us directly. That's why Buddhas appear in human form — because we can actually see those. We can't see their enjoyment body, we can't see their truth body.

So yeah, those two are perfect choices. But then we should think, if they're good choices, then I have to find how they're appearing in my world. And I want to go find that person and have a chat with them and get help from them, so that I can get direct help. That's our own personal choice. As you mentioned, many people choose Venerable Geshe-la — a very good choice. But of course, we have freedom to choose whoever we'd like.

The last thing about this is that we need the ability to see Buddhas in this world. So part of the practice of reliance on a spiritual guide is actually learning to see purity in the world. If we can't see purity in at least one person, in the form of our spiritual guide, then we'll never see purity in ourselves or other people. We'll never be able to see anyone as a Buddha.

So part of the practice — it's actually a tantric practice — is learning to see beyond the ordinary. And often, the human that we choose as the spiritual guide is basically the first person we get really good at seeing beyond the ordinary with. And that person is a paradigm, or an example, that we then apply to all other living beings one day, including ourself.

So that practice is very important. We can't not do that practice if we want to develop pure view one day. The reason that person is the easiest is because they seem to have the most Buddha-like qualities we can muster up. So that is a basis of imputation that gives us the freedom to impute Buddha.

It's hard sometimes to do it with ourself, because we see all the delusions and nonsense and whatever. You can do it through tantric practice, but it takes a little bit of wisdom and skill. That's hard to do with our crazy friends and family members and whatever else, because they really don't seem much like a Buddha.

So we have to find — where is the most valid basis of imputation for Buddha I can find? And it's on that person that we start practicing seeing beyond the ordinary and seeing purity. And in that way, that person is really guiding us to enlightenment by being the example that allows us to see beyond the ordinary. And then we can do it with all living beings. Anyway, please, Ryan.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: Just a quick follow-up. But as for me, Geshe-la — I never met him in real life, and he doesn't live anymore. So I can't say that I would find someone who lives now as an emanation, a really human person. So I am back to — even some people, I know like you, you have met him and other people. But for me, I never met him in real life. So I'm like back to ground zero. Where can I find a real living?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. Because you lived at the same time as him, you can choose him. And you have met him — because his books. It's like he often said, these are me. My books are me. And so if you've met his books, and you've benefited from practicing these texts, then you've met him directly, and been helped by him directly. But yeah, you can also choose someone else. But just always remember that their power is coming basically essentially through him. Anne has a hand there.

teaching.speaker: Anne K
teaching.text: This is very related to Ryan's question. So given I'm on board with the idea that we need to find someone living to be our spiritual guide, given the fact that Je Tsongkhapa and Geshe Kelsang are both no longer living, why is at this point one preferable to the other as a spiritual guide?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, because part of it is because Geshe-la was with us here, and was alive while we were alive. I think we were all alive while he was alive. So he was part of our world, our reality, working with us, helping us directly. And because he's sort of the mouthpiece for Je Tsongkhapa for us now. So that would be why he would be a very good choice.

But yeah, of course we have freedom. So we could relate to one of his disciples as a spiritual guide for us who's living right now. But we would just always want to remember that person is getting all their power through him and through Je Tsongkhapa. So it's always going back to all the Buddhas.

Yeah, thanks, Ryan, for asking that. Do we know the story of Sadaprarudita? Anyone? No? Might as well read that, because it's very relevant. It's actually coming up pretty soon in the text, but I'll just — oh no, it's not that soon. Okay, I'll just read it out.

Geshe-la says here, page 127, Meaningful to Behold. 'In the final chapters of the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, Buddha Shakyamuni tells the following story of Bodhisattva Sadaprarudita, who perfected the practice of selfless giving as part of his spiritual path.

Sadaprarudita was a sincere practitioner who, like a thirsty person in search of water, looked everywhere for a teacher who could explain to him the profound view of emptiness. One day he heard a voice from the sky tell him to go to the east, where a great teacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, lived. For he was the guru who could teach him.

Sadaprarudita became very happy at the thought that he would now receive teachings. As a sign of his sincerity and devotion, he wanted to bring the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata an offering of gold and silver, but was too poor to afford even the smallest gift. At that time the thought came to his mind: the only thing of value that I possess is my body. I will sell this, and with the money I receive, I will be able to buy offerings for my teacher.

He immediately went to a nearby town and stood in the street and cried out, who will buy my body? I will sell it to whoever wants it. Yet despite his loud and desperate cries, no one came forward to take up his offer.'

You can imagine what happened in downtown Brooklyn. This thing probably happens a couple of times a day.

'Depressed that now there was no way for him to raise the money for his teacher's gift, Sadaprarudita sat down and began to cry. From his abode in the celestial realms, the great Lord Indra, chief of the gods, saw all that had happened and decided to test the young Bodhisattva. Transforming himself into a high caste Brahmin, Indra appeared before Sadaprarudita and asked why he was crying.

When the Bodhisattva explained his plight and why he needed the money, the Brahmin said: normally I have no need for human flesh and blood. It so happens, however, that today I must perform a special sacrifice and need unusual ingredients. Therefore, I would gladly pay for some of your flesh.

Sadaprarudita was ecstatic that he had finally found someone to whom he could sell his body. He started to cut some flesh from his right thigh and, picking up a large rock, was about to break the bones of his leg. The daughter of a local merchant lived in a house nearby and witnessed the unusual scene taking place out in the street.

Greatly alarmed, she ran outside and asked the Bodhisattva why he was mutilating himself so horribly. Sadaprarudita calmly explained that he was selling his flesh so that he could make offerings to the teacher Dharmodgata in order to receive the wisdom teachings from him. What is the great benefit of these teachings for you to harm yourself this way? she asked.

The Bodhisattva replied that by meditating upon the teachings on emptiness one could attain the full enlightenment of Buddhahood. The merchant's daughter then asked about Buddhahood and the young Bodhisattva explained to her all the excellent qualities of a fully enlightened being' — to make an offering worthy of the great teacher Dharmodgata.

'Seeing the Bodhisattva's willingness to sacrifice himself and listening to his conversation with the merchant's daughter, the great god Indra realized the extent and the depth of his great compassion. He immediately transformed himself back into his original shape and proclaimed: all the Buddhas of the past attained their enlightenment with the great mind and effort that you now possess. It is truly wonderful that for the sake of Dharma you are prepared to sacrifice your body. Please tell me if there is anything in the entire universe that I can give you now.'

So Indra is like the king of the gods. Much more powerful than anyone we have ever met or can imagine.

'Sadaprarudita replied: the only thing I require is the path that leads to enlightenment. Hearing this, Indra was forced to admit: I can give you anything in the universe, but only an enlightened being has the power to fulfill your request. And the Bodhisattva made the following prayer: if without deception I gave my body for the sake of Dharma, then through the power of that pure offering, may I be restored to full health. Instantly upon the conclusion of this prayer, his body was made whole again.

The merchant's daughter escorted the Bodhisattva into her house and asked her father to give Sadaprarudita gold and silver as an offering to his teacher. When the merchant heard his daughter's story, he too was filled with strong devotion' — oh gosh, actually a lot more — 'and bestowed upon the Bodhisattva five hundred carts laden with gold and silver and delectable food.'

I'm going to expedite this now. So eventually he met Dharmodgata, and hearing the teachings he gained a direct realization of emptiness. It was so beautiful. And then Dharmodgata entered into a long meditation and remained in that state for seven years, and Sadaprarudita waited to receive more teachings. He didn't think about food and drink but waited patiently, intent on receiving more teachings.

When he arose from his meditation, he requested more teachings and began to prepare a large area with suitable offerings. There was dust everywhere and he wanted to clean it, so he even cut his body and used the blood to settle the dust on the ground.

Anyway, it goes on and on, and eventually finally Sadaprarudita himself attained the eighth of the ten Bodhisattva grounds and suddenly flew up into the sky to go see his teacher. When he asked him why all these miracles had occurred, Dharmodgata replied that this was an auspicious indication of the great benefit received that day. Owing to Sadaprarudita's request and Dharmodgata's own teaching, many thousands of beings received the correct view of emptiness and developed the precious mind of bodhichitta.

So obviously the moral of the story isn't to chop our body up, but it's to think about him as a perfect example of what a mind that appreciates a spiritual guide looks like. You know, it looks radical from one point of view, but from another point of view it makes the most sense. Like his total, absolute fervor for finding and relying on a spiritual guide who could lead him to the correct view of emptiness — with no interest in wealth or reputation or whatever, just only wanting those wisdom teachings.

So this is a famous story that's in the Perfection of Wisdom Sutras. And his name, Sadaprarudita, means 'the one who was always crying,' because up until he found Dharmodgata, his guru, he just wept all the time. He couldn't stop crying because he was dying to meet a guru who could guide him to those teachings. So may we have that same value of our own spiritual guide.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, that's good for now. Let's have a little time for discussion. Anne and Mary Ann and Byron and Jose and Fran and David and Anne P, Mimi and Ryan.

smallGroupDiscussion.note: Small group discussion on the eight precepts of aspiring bodhichitta. Transcript heavily garbled due to overlapping speakers and ambient audio. Groups discussed why each of the eight precepts was specifically chosen for preventing degeneration of the aspiring mind.

practiceAgreement.speaker: Suzanne
practiceAgreement.text: I just love the idea of all week not to abandon any living being. Like, wow, to just keep that in my heart all day long. Any living being.

practiceAgreement.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceAgreement.text:
Yeah, it's a good idea. Basically taking one of the eight aspiring vows and trying to really work on one of them. Because it's a little bit daunting to do all eight right away. Even like, for example, to just emphasize getting merit and wisdom — that's a whole full-time task. Or to just constantly trust or rely on our spiritual guide. Or to not abandon any living being.

So it'd be nice for us each — maybe we can all choose one that speaks to us. It could just be the six-times-a-day ones, or whatever, and then really go wild on it for the week. Anyone against that? Okay. Adriana, yeah.

practiceAgreement.speaker: Adriana
practiceAgreement.text: Dale and I started thinking about little incremental steps to develop those four characteristics of the Buddha. That was helpful.

practiceAgreement.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceAgreement.text: Yeah, that would be another nice thing — to kind of grow our skill, to become more omniscient, oppose our obstacles to liberation and omniscience, to become more impartial, and to not just help people who helped us but want to help everyone equally. Yeah, it'd be nice to move the marker on those a little bit forward for each one of us.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Okay, we'll dedicate in a moment. I was just thinking back to that feeling of being in the living presence of your spiritual guide. I think I mentioned this before, but for me, when I — I relied on Venerable Geshe-la as my guru for three years before I met him. And then I met him in Portugal at the temple opening. He was sort of at the bottom of the drive. I was up a hill.

And seeing the living spiritual guide — for me, there was no conceptual activity. There was just the deepest weeping from my soul I've ever experienced in my whole life. Not that much of a crier. And even when I am, it's not like that. But I just wept from the absolute depths of my soul, of my being, uncontrollably for a very long time.

And that was a very nice experience — this feeling of, oh, I'm in the living presence of my spiritual guide. I already had a devout, devotional relationship and a sincere relying, but the sense of, I'm in the living presence. There was something about, this person is living in my world. They're alive. There's someone I could talk to and interact with. Or they've been present and touched the ground that I'm walking on. That sense is very special and beautiful. And then everything feels possible when we feel that way.

Okay, so we can just dedicate here. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications. Okay, thank you. Thanks, everyone. See you next week.
